pedigree_analysis.title: Family History Interpretation
pedigree_analysis.content:
Autosomal Dominant
• Vertical transmission
• 50% offspring risk
• Example: Huntington's disease
X-linked Recessive
• Male predominance
• No male-to-male transmission
• Example: Duchenne muscular dystrophy

molecular_pathology.title: Genotype-Phenotype Correlations
molecular_pathology.content:
Cystic Fibrosis

Gene: CFTR (7q31.2)

ΔF508 Mutation: Protein misfolding → chloride channel defect

Triad: Chronic lung disease, pancreatic insufficiency, ↑sweat Cl-

Marfan Syndrome

Gene: FBN1 (fibrillin-1)

Effect: Connective tissue weakness

Diagnosis: Ghent criteria (aortic root dilation + ectopia lentis)

diagnostic_approaches.title: Genetic Testing Modalities
diagnostic_approaches.content:
• Karyotyping: Aneuploidy detection (resolution 5-10 Mb)
  • FISH: Targeted microdeletions (e.g., 22q11.2)
  • CMA: Genome-wide CNVs (resolution 50-100 kb)
  • NGS: Panel/WES/WGS (single nucleotide resolution)

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why are autosomal dominant disorders often late-onset?

Many involve gain-of-function or toxic aggregation (e.g., huntingtin protein) that takes decades to manifest, unlike recessive loss-of-function disorders presenting in childhood.

How can identical mutations cause different disease severity?

Due to modifier genes (e.g., α-thalassemia ameliorates β-thalassemia) or environmental factors (diet in PKU).

Why are mitochondrial disorders multisystemic?

High-energy tissues (brain, muscle, retina) are most vulnerable to ATP production defects from mtDNA mutations.
